0Yves here. It should be noted that the US has maintained financial/economic dominance in what looked like (from the perspective of US elites and other capital-owners) a virtuous circle. The dollar was the reserve currency by virtue of the US running sustained trade deficits, which is tantamount to exporting jobs. Many of the exporting countries (despite World Bank efforts to have them establish capital markets) do not have sufficiently deep or liquid securities markets to serve as a meaningful repository for domestic investment. As happens where I am now, real estate investment takes place at a level that leads to widespread overvaluation, and a lot of capital is also invested abroad. US financial markets were and even now still are the cleanest and most liquid in the world, so it remains a relatively attractively outlet for investment (the dollar and dollar markets are still the cleanest shirt in the dirty laundry). Keep in mind that dollar reinvestment does not take place only via purchasing US securities but also real estate, investment in private companies, and direct investment.
In addition, many developing countries chose to accumulate large foreign exchange reserves, predominantly in dollars, after the 1997 Asian crisis, so as to make sure they would not again need an IMF rescue.
So one can argue that as the dollar model evolved, it depended on the US ability to continue running trade surpluses. That would have required some attention to the economic health of US consumers and businesses, as in assuring rising real incomes (albeit less high than if the US was not exporting jobs). Instead, the US went full bore for neoliberalism, which included indifference to rentierism, particularly in health care, housing, and higher education, while also tolerating, even promoting, de-industrialization.
By Glenn Diesen. Originally published at his channel
Glenn Diesen
Welcome back. Professor Michael Hudson joins us today, and I would advise everyone to follow his work. I’ve left a link in the description. So yes, at least this is what I read to stay up to date. Thank you for coming back on, Michael. It’s great to see you again. 
Michael Hudson
It’s good to be here with all of this news happening. The stock market’s up. Everybody seems confident that there’s not going to be much of a disturbance in world inflation or exchange rates from all of this. It’s just amazing. Well, we’re talking about the war that’s going on, the market as if, well, it’s really not going to matter.
Glenn Diesen
I’m wondering if they’re delusional or if it’s market manipulation, or how to explain this. Anyway, that’s some of the things we’re getting to today. Because what is happening is quite remarkable. After decades of globalization—that is, the integration of markets and also a buildup of huge, unsustainable debt—we now see that this US-centric format for globalization, that is, integrating the world organized around the United States, this model has seemingly exhausted itself. That is, it’s organized around US financial markets, the US dollar, US-controlled transportation corridors. All of this is now being dismantled by economic warfare and even war. And you probably saw in the interview with Scott Besant, where he makes the point that the wars on Iran, Venezuela, even Russia, they all have an economic function to strengthen the US dollar. So I thought it was interesting because it does beg the question: to what extent is anyone behind the wheel, or do you see a plan here of the United States?
Michael Hudson
Well, there has been a long plan, and it’s very easy to dismiss Trump and say, well, Trump’s losing the war with Iran. The whole memorandum of understanding was, in effect, a capitulation to Iran. And you can see that it seems futile for Trump to try to get in deeper and deeper. So the assumption is, since he’s getting the U.S. in deeper and deeper, he must not have a plan because it’s not working. But there is a plan, and not only Trump, but especially his colleague, Secretary of the Treasury Besant, has been very openly expressing what this is. And Trump himself was outlining the plan already in his first administration, way back in 2018. He said that the number one aim was that he saw America’s military spending abroad, in an attempt to enforce a U.S.-centered world order— dollarization, U.S. financial markets—had been, since 1950, the main balance of payments drain on the United States. And it was foreign military spending that forced the United States off gold in 1971. Well, from 1971 until very recently, what took the place of gold? The U.S. spent money into foreign markets, and foreign markets were recycling this to the United States. At first, local recipients of dollars—companies, economies, governments—would turn over the dollars to the central bank. And what would the central bank do? Well, as we’ve discussed before, and as I discussed in my book *Superimperialism*, foreign central banks bought U.S. Treasury IOUs— Treasury bonds, securities, notes, short-term. And then, in the last few years, instead of this intergovernmental central bank recycling, you had foreign private investors buying U.S. stocks and U. S. bonds. All of this money was recycled into the U.S. stock market, which was mainly being driven up by debt. Well, all of this means of somehow maintaining America’s domination is now called into question. What Trump had said is, well, the first thing we want to do is stop all of this military spending we’re doing abroad. He’d talked about withdrawing his troops from NATO already in his first administration, and he’d singled out OPEC. He said, we’re spending a lot of money defending the Middle East, West Asia, and they really have to somehow end up paying us. Well, of course, that was the whole idea of the petrodollar agreement of 1974–1975, that OPEC could charge whatever it wanted for its oil, and it would reinvest its oil earnings in the U.S. financial markets, stocks, and bonds. Well, all of that was working. But still, the United States, in the interim since the 1970s, has lost its industrial power. It’s lost its creditor power, turning into a debtor country. It needed a new strategy. And last year, at the end of 2025, the U.S. spelled out the strategy. And it was, well, we can’t support our control of the world economy anymore by industry or even by our financial markets. We have to establish a series of monopolies to make America a rentier economy. And the three sectors that the United States wanted to control have been, number one, the longstanding sector of oil. We’ve discussed that before. America wants to control the oil trade so that its allies cannot deal with other producers of oil that would interfere with the U.S. monopoly. So while almost all the attention of the shows that you’ve been doing and that have been in the media has been focused on the fighting against Iran and isolating Iranian oil, especially Iranian oil exports to China, there’s been a similar U.S. attack bombing Russian oil refineries and gas refineries through Ukraine. The United States has been providing Ukraine with guidance and missiles to show just exactly where to bomb so that Russia will not be the beneficiary of this imminent rise in oil prices that’s going to result from the closing of the Strait of Hormuz for 20% of the world’s oil trade, and now another 5% of the world’s oil trade as the Yemenis have cut back Saudi Arabia’s West Coast export facilities. So the world is facing a very sharp rise in oil prices.
And essentially, the United States wants to be the beneficiary of this, especially through the exportation of natural gas, liquefied natural gas. So it wants to make sure that it will be the beneficiary of this rise in oil prices as a result of the war in West Asia, not Russia, and still wants to be able to isolate China from receiving this. Well, what Trump has done, early this year he said what he really wants to do, repeatedly, is make the Arab OPEC countries pay for America’s military costs there. Well, suddenly, Trump was inspired by the fact that Iran now wants to impose tolls on traffic through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran has estimated will yield it about $40 billion a year. Well, Trump finally has found a way to charge the OPEC countries for the costs of the military. He calls it defense, or a guardian angel, defending these countries from Iran and any other attacker. And he said, well, there will be—he said a few days ago—there are going to be tolls in the Strait of Hormuz. Forget international law about no tolls being allowed to be imposed on international waters. There are going to be tolls. We will get them, not Iran. Well, immediately Secretary of State Rubio said, wait a minute, if you’re saying that America will get the tolls instead of Iran, then that justifies Iran’s claim that the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea is dead. The UN rules that international waters cannot have tolls unless they’ve been grandfathered in by signatories to the UN agreement, such as Turkey with access to the Black Sea, Egypt with its canal, and the Panama Canal. Unless they’ve grandfathered these in, international waters can’t have tolls. Well, Rubio said, you can’t say this. We don’t want to give up anything on international law that we can still use to try to prevent Iran from getting the tolls. So Trump then backpedaled, and the next day, a few days ago, gave a press conference saying, all right, we’ve made a new agreement with the OPEC Arab countries. They are going to pay us for the cost of our defending them as their guardian angel, but not through tolls. They’re going to invest in the United States, just as way back after 1975, Saudi Arabia and the OPEC countries invested their oil export earnings here. They’re going to invest in U.S. industry as partners. And already this has begun to take form. Amazon, for instance, has made a huge investment in Bahrain in artificial intelligence, these huge fields of computers that are using energy. And that is the second element of what the U.S. wants to monopolize. In addition to controlling the oil trade and essentially obtaining all of the recycled oil export revenues for its own economy, the U.S. wants to control a monopoly in information technology and associated computerization and the Internet. And this is why what has been stabilizing the U.S. balance of payments has been huge private foreign investment and government investment, including the United Arab Emirates, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, into the U.S. golden seven stocks of information technology, computer chips, and Amazon and Google and all of the Internet and public discussions, X, etc., Facebook, all of these. Well, the problem is now that these stocks are going down because analysts have found out, well, in order for these companies to make this vast increase in earnings, in monopoly rents that they’ve expected as a result of building huge information technology centers, we can’t do that in the United States because we don’t have the electricity and we don’t have the water to cool the electricity, the chips that make all this intelligence. So just as the United States has offshored its industry, its manufacturing industry, it’s now offshoring its artificial intelligence monopoly. Where is it going to offshore it to? Well, to the OPEC countries, especially to the Arab OPEC countries. That’s why, as I said, Amazon and Bahrain. And in the last two days, the United States has made a deal with the Arab Emirates saying, well, you know, you can be partners with us in huge U.S. investments in building these industries together, this information technology where you are. You will provide the… You won’t have to export your energy at all. You’ll provide your energy domestically to power this huge American investment in information technology. Well, a few days ago, Iran focused its bombing on Amazon’s investment in information technology in Bahrain. Iran’s position is, well, what’s our strategy? Number one, we want to drive the United States out of the whole West Asian region. The first thing we’ve got to do is drive out the military bases. It’s done that with all the military bases except Israel. It’s bombed them, and the United States Army, the military, is in complete agreement: okay, we’re going to withdraw our military bases there. We can’t afford them anymore, mainly because we can’t protect them from the Iranian missiles that have shown they can penetrate our defenses at will. And Iran has just finished, in the last three days, bombing what’s left of the American military bases. But Iran then says, if we are going to drive the United States out of West Asia, it can’t just be the military bases. We have to end the whole economic and financial symbiosis between the United States and these local monarchies there. And under this symbiosis of investing their oil export proceeds in American stocks and bonds and partnerships with the American AI industry, their hearts are going to follow where the money is. We’ve got to prevent this economic symbiosis. So there’s not going to be any linkage at all between the U.S. economy and these economies, so that we can then essentially free the region from the United States. Well, that means that its bombing is going to prevent all of this. This is really what the war is all about, and it’s been depicted as an existential war on Iran’s part because the United States wanted to do to Iran just what it did to Mexico. It wanted to have a very quick war, as it had in Venezuela. You kidnap the president, you have a regime change that agrees to turn over its oil to the United States. All of Venezuela’s oil export revenues are put into a U.S. bank account that’s run by the U.S. Treasury. Well, a few months ago, the Secretary of the Treasury, Besant, said, we’re going to do the same thing in Iran once we defeat it. And just before the June 17th Memorandum of Understanding was signed, Hegseth came out and said, well, what we’re going to do is we’re going to conquer Iran, and we’re going to have a regime change that will put all of Iran’s oil revenues in a Treasury account, and this account will have to be spent in the United States to buy U.S. exports and U.S. goods. Well, then the negotiators worked out this memorandum of agreement, and it looks like Iran has just withdrawn from that agreement a few days ago because it became apparent that the United States never had any intention at all of actually meeting the terms of the agreement. For one thing, the whole agreement was to be put in motion by this payment of at least a token sum of $12 billion of the $100 billion of Iranian savings that the United States has told its allies, especially in the Emirates and the Arab OPEC countries, to confiscate. Well, Hegseth said he’s worked with the Emirates to say, don’t give them a penny. And so the Emirates and Bahrain and other countries have said, we’re not going to return any of this $12 billion, much less $100 billion.
To Iran, we’re going to say, Iran, you’ve attacked us. When we attack you, you fought back. Your fighting back is an attack on us. We want reparations for the cost that we’ve had to suffer from your defending yourself against the U.S., Israeli, and our own military attacks on you. And Hegseth had spelled all this out just before, actually on July 11th, when the negotiators drafted the agreement that was signed on the 17th. Well, it’s obvious this wasn’t going to be enacted. And regarding letting Iran administer trade in the Strait of Hormuz, the United States never had any intention at all of letting Iran charge any tolls or even administrative fees for registering the ships, for coordinating the ships—anything that the administration of a strait would do. The U.S. Navy came in and protected ships to try to break Iranian control by turning off their transponders and sailing close to the Omani shore, saying, well, you know, even though the Memorandum of Understanding said Iran will govern all shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, this doesn’t apply to Iran’s own territorial waters. So there are going to be two routes through the Strait of Hormuz. There’s going to be the Iranian shore route that’s not international waters, and it’s not under Iranian waters. And as for the in between international waters, that doesn’t apply because the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea, UNCLOS, prevents any country from charging tolls that isn’t already grandfathered into the clause. And Iran said, well, we never signed that agreement. Iran may have, but it hasn’t us. And Iran is in a state of war with us. And anyway, this law of the sea saying you can’t charge tolls does not preclude us and other countries from defending ourselves in a state of war. Oman is in a state of war with us because Oman is hosting U.S. military bases from which missiles and bombs are being sent into our territory. So, of course, we have control over the strait. Well, this is what Trump is all about. So Iran is claiming the right to claim it when the 60-day ceasefire period was to have been over. Iran had planned to impose these tolls. Trump said, no, you’re not going to impose the tolls. We’re going to impose the tolls to reimburse ourselves for all of the costs. And we’re going to get 20% of the oil export proceeds of the Arab countries who export this oil—20% of the value of this is all going to be paid to us as a toll. Well, that’s what immediately the legal fight is about. There goes the international law of the sea. There goes the memorandum of understanding. So you see that when this is the aim of Trump, you could say that he’s attacking Iran not simply because he’s deluded by his belief that somehow we can destroy Iran’s military, we can destroy their defenses, we can destroy their missiles, we can hit the civilians and the hospitals and the schools and demoralize the population so much that they will want to put a U.S. regime in so we’ll stop making them so unhappy. This is all an illusion. But for the U.S., this fight against Iran is extraordinary—existential for the United States’ plan of how to control the world economy, as it is for Iran to defend its own sovereignty and its own existence against the United States’ attempt to invade it, break it up by trying to get the invasions from Balochistan, from the Kurds, and others. So this is really what the fight is all about and why it’s going to go on and on. And in the process of going on and on, it will block the oil trade, leading to a stoppage of oil, leading to the world production crisis and financial crisis that we’ve discussed in our earlier shows.
Glenn Diesen
Well, I’m thinking if I was in Washington advising Trump on how to restore U.S. geoeconomic dominance, I would probably advise what they’re doing now to a large extent. That is, for the U.S. to revive its technological dominance, for it to control international transportation corridors—that is, the maritime corridors, etc.—restore, yeah, third, restore America’s financial dominance with its currency. You know, you want to keep rivals of the United States weakened, you want to keep the rivals divided, prevent them from integrating, and also keep the vassals dependent. If you do want to find a new formula for American dominance, that seems to be a good pathway now. As you say, they do very often make comments that support this logic, though. That is, the idea that all international waterways must remain under U.S. control, even through piracy. We see now part of the way they measured success in Venezuela was, that they will now have to sell their oil in dollars. Their proceeds will have to be invested into the United States. Trump himself bragged about how much money they’ve been able to extract from Venezuela. We see the same with Russia, how much there are comments about torching Russian oil refineries through their Ukrainian proxy. Besant made the comment that after the war, the Russians will probably be forced to start selling their oil and gas in dollars again. And, um, yeah, Iran, as Lindsey Gray made the point, that yes, Iran is oil-rich, and this will now fall under U.S. control when it’s over. We had all these American leaders at some point making the same chant, that is, you know, this short-term pain for long-term gain—we’re going to get it under our control. Not just American control, but the oil would have to be sold—well, the part of the deal the Americans wanted, which they were quite open about, was that whatever the Iranians make from oil, which should be sold in dollars, should be used to give the U.S. exclusive rights to sell agricultural products to Iran. So again, selling in dollars, used to buy U.S. products. And at the same time, when the Americans are punishing Iran, they’re torching all the bridges and things that are used to connect the Eurasian landmass that is part of the Belt and Road Initiative, which connects Iran to Russia, China, and so forth. We see that the allies or vassals of the United States in the Middle East and Europe are now asked to increase their dependence on the U.S., and the U.S. will also monetize this. That is, they now have to pay for, quote-unquote, protection. We see the same with all these wars on Iran, for example, that China should be cut off from a key supplier of oil. It should also, of course, have its tech development scaled back to restore U.S. tech dominance. So I see what they’re going for, and if we throw all the morals out the window, global hegemony is the key objective. All of this makes perfect sense. The fact that they’re saying it out loud as well is quite interesting. But I guess my question is, what is the likelihood of the U.S. succeeding in these objectives, and what could go wrong? Because the U.S. wanted to break Chinese tech dominance, it proved that that wasn’t really feasible. They also see that Russia is willing to go all the way. Essentially, Iran isn’t being defeated. They’re not giving up. They see what the Americans are doing. The Iranians, as you said, are willing to destroy data centers of the United States in the Middle East. They’re willing to knock out—I think they took out the desalination plant in Kuwait—which means they can actually make this country cease to exist. They’re willing to go up that escalation ladder because it’s all or nothing for them. So I guess my question is, to what extent do you see the U.S. being able to control the economic consequences of these conflicts, that is, these wars, be they economic or actual wars against China, Russia, Iran? Because a lot of things can go wrong, and at the same time, the U.S. economy isn’t doing that well either. I mean, yes, the stock markets are up, and if that was the only indicator of economic health, wonderful—America would be back. But, you know, many things can go wrong here.
Michael Hudson
Well, you’re right to have mentioned transportation. And to answer your question, in order to impose U.S. control of the world oil trade to get its income for itself, and the artificial intelligence computer technology trade, the U.S. does need to control shipping and international transportation as well. Because how can you export your oil without doing it by ships or by overland means such as pipelines? Well, the very first fight that Trump picked with Europe and most of America’s main—I won’t say enemy, but its main opponent—is, of course, Europe, its allies, Europe, Japan, and its other allies. Before it fights its real enemies—Russia, China, and Iran—and the global majority, it wants to tighten its control over Europe and make sure that Europe is locked into dependence on America’s liquefied natural gas and transportation. And so this required two things: number one, the blowing up of the North Sea pipeline, as we’ve discussed; and number two, what you’re seeing now—the constant bombing of Russian shipping through the Baltic. For a long time, Russia exported its oil through the Latvian east coast vents, that went through the Baltic. Russia is now still exporting oil through the Baltic, and you have Estonia and Latvia, permitting NATO to basically stop Russian oil exports through the Baltic. Well, all of that violates the UN Law of the Sea. That’s not free trade. The United States’ objective now is saying, in 1945, we supported free trade because we were the beneficiaries. When England promoted free trade in the 19th century, that was called free trade imperialism. Well, that’s what America did after 1945. But now we’re not for free trade anymore, because if we can’t have free trade of other countries trading among themselves and being independent of the United States—if we can’t control foreign oil as a rival—we will destroy that oil. We will destroy Russia’s ability to refine its oil. We will destroy Russia’s ability to transport its oil to other countries. We will destroy its pipelines. And the same with Iran. We will destroy Iranian ports and Iranian shipping, as we’ve been doing, so that it can’t export either to China or to India or anywhere else. So the control of oil and control of transportation go together. Well, that’s why the first fight Trump had with Europe was over Greenland. We’ve got to take control of Greenland because then, if we can have a link from Greenland to Iceland to Britain, we can block access from the North Atlantic Ocean into the Arctic. And if we can block that access, then Europe and West Asia won’t have access to the Arctic trade to avoid conflict, having to go around through South Africa or having to go around the U.S.-controlled Panama Canal. We’ve been able to block the oil trade and any other trade from there. Well, I’m a little surprised. Russia has been trying to arrange with China the Power of Siberia pipeline to say, well, look, the United States is trying to—in violation of the Law of the Sea, in violation of all of the free trade rules—it’s preventing us from shipping our oil. So the only way to get around it is through a pipeline. And that’s, of course, what China has been trying to do through its Belt and Road Initiative, essentially to integrate Eurasia, the whole Asian continent, so that it doesn’t need to have the Mackinder strategy of controlling the periphery. But China and Russia have argued over what’s going to be the price for the oil. Well, Russia quite correctly says, well, we can see that the price of oil is going to go up because it looks now like the United States is goading Iran and the Arab countries to destroy each other’s oil production, while NATO is fighting against Russia to destroy its oil export capacity. And without OPEC oil, there’s going to be a huge oil shortage. And the United States will supply this basically through shipping gas to countries that need this energy. This is why Trump has fought against alternatives to oil in the form of wind energy and solar energy, which China has dominated in. So that’s the link between transport. And now for your question, how can this succeed? Well, it can only succeed by—let’s start with the American fight against Europe to subordinate its allies, Europe and Japan, to the United States. The whole assumption, the materialist approach to history, is that countries are going to act in their economic self-interest. Well, Europe isn’t acting in its economic self-interest. That would be to get inexpensive energy to power its industry and avoid the deindustrialization that you’re seeing in Germany and other NATO countries. It can’t afford the higher prices of oil, and its chemical industry can’t afford to operate at a profit when there is an interruption of the derivatives of the oil trade— sulfur to make sulfuric acid for mining, and fertilizer made out of natural gas. Not to mention helium—one of the first production sites that Iran hit was Qatar’s helium production, which was itself 20% of the world’s helium trade—totally destroyed. It cost, I think, $5 billion to install originally and took a number of years to complete. All of this is unavailable for the next few years, causing a helium shortage. China and the United States are major producers of helium. China has stopped its helium exports, and the United States is now using its helium monopoly as a lever of international control. So the United States retains a lot of levers and control. And the ultimate, the fourth monopoly that we didn’t discuss, is the U.S. dollarization— the financial system monopoly. This is what we’ve been discussing for the last few shows that you’ve had me on. The United States tried to exclude its rivals from the SWIFT bank clearing system. China set up an alternative to that. Everything the United States has done by imposing financial sanctions on other countries is to try to say, well, we can cut off your financial payments. But how can there be an oil trade? How can there be a trade in industrial products if you can’t process the payment for it? You not only need to transport this trade, you need to transfer the monetary payments. We’re controlling that system too. The whole American strategy is no longer a win-win strategy between it and the rest of the world. It’s about what choke points we can use to control the world economy—whether they can get oil and energy to power their factories, light their homes, and supply their chemical and fertilizer industry, information technology, and grain. Well, to answer your question, the American strategy can only succeed as long as the United States can impose choke points on the entire world—either by imposing sanctions that other countries will not have an alternative means of becoming independent from, with their own alternatives to the sanctions, their own payment systems such as China has been developing, their oil production like Russia and Iran, their transportation like the Arctic route of transport, and the Russian ability to fight NATO military attacks on Russian shipping through the Baltic and other areas, and U.S. attacks on shipping through the Indian Ocean that it’s been doing. The answer to whether the U.S. can maintain its control and its new, almost neocolonial imperialism depends on its ability to make a win-lose situation—trade on the world, saying, if you want oil, you’ll have to pay our monopoly oil prices, and the profits that the oil producers make will all be invested in the United States or spent on U.S. exports. To ship, you’ll have to submit to U.S. permission to use U.S.-controlled ports or routes that we’re closing off if you’re not subordinate to us for information technology, where we’ve imposed sanctions. Well, just yesterday, the United States lifted sanctions on exporting the most advanced computer chips to the Emirates. And it’s done that so that the Emirates can invest with the United States. This is tens of billions of dollars to create these new computer chip transfer centers, like the Amazon Cloud Investment Center in Bahrain was supposed to have done. All of the ideas that somehow they’ve convinced the Emirates to throw in their lot with the United States. And the United States gave the Emirates this permission in exchange for its agreement to help the United States bomb Iran. Well, all of this, the success of this U.S. policy, depends on how long the Arab Middle East can be ruled by these rotten semi-feudal monarchies. How long can the Emirates survive? How long can Jordan survive? Bahrain, Saudi Arabia itself, survived when most of the population is either Palestinian or Indian, where you have a very unequal society, by emirates who basically control the economies and have thrown in their lot with the United States. Almost every war, the backwash of a war, has been settled by huge political upheavals. World War I saw the end of many European monarchies and the transition to some sort of constitutional monarchy or quasi democracy. The Ottoman Empire was broken up and made into colonies of Britain and France, and basically that redrew the map, carved up the Ottoman Empire. Well, the question is, now that this war is over, is there going to be a similar political revolution going throughout West Asia, establishing economies that actually use their oil, not to recycle their economic surpluses to the United States leader, not to fall into the position that countries like Germany or Britain are in as just being satellites of the United States, and certainly not Japan, that America is trying to get rearmed to serve the United States? Are they going to go down the same route as Japan, Britain, and Germany? Or somehow is there going to be a social revolution there, like America feared would be the case after World War II? Are we finally going to see the carve-up that occurred after World War I with the Sykes plan to redraw the lines and put in British- and French-installed local monarchies? Are we finally going to see them brought into the modern progressive era? That’s going to be part of the question — whether the United States plan can stop progress. Can the United States stop the rest of the world from acting in its own economic self-interest to promote its own development instead of being subservient to promote the U.S. economy, which will not use this income for its own development, but really just to increase its monopoly, control, and military threat to other countries? That’s really the question.
Glenn Diesen
Yeah, well, that’s a good point. That is, the ability of the U.S. to restore its dominance doesn’t only depend on the ability of its rivals to fight back, which they are, but indeed on its allies accepting very destructive vassalage, as you see in the Middle East. I mean, they’re paying a high price for their partnership with the U.S. now. And it’s quite different, the relationship with the United States than in the past, because after World War II, the U.S. free trade empire — I mean, yeah, for example, the Europeans were completely subordinated to the U.S. However, at least it was beneficial to some extent. The U.S. was considered a benign hegemon. That is, we made sure that its frontline states were prosperous. That is, that the West Germans were more prosperous than East Germans, the South Koreans were more prosperous than North Koreans, and the Taiwanese Chinese were more prosperous than mainland Chinese. So, you know, the frontline states were thriving. But now, as the U.S. can’t afford this format for its dominance anymore, it begins to cannibalize its rivals, demand excessive vassalage. And as you said, I think the core is how do you make states not act in their own interest. This is important because if you look at the European case study now, I mean, they’re not acting in their own interest. Their economies are getting weaker. They’re politically getting weaker. They’re having a legitimacy crisis because, you know, in a redivided Europe, it’s not in Europe’s interest anymore. It creates conflicts and war with the Russians, which enhances the dependence on the U.S., makes them economically weak. And if you see the leadership across Europe, I mean, it’s like a competition — how unpopular can you possibly get? And in this legitimacy crisis, you will inevitably see new political alternatives emerge. A good example is Germany with the AfD, growing out of nothing to becoming the most popular party. Well, what are they saying? They’re saying we should act in our own interest. And what is that? We’ll have to diversify energy supplies, have to make peace with Russia. And other interests will be in diversified technology, work with China as well, diversify transportation corridors, diversify finance. In other words, don’t tie yourself only to the United States. And I think it’s going to be hard for the United States to continue this position because as long as vassals can’t act in their own interest, the whole thing becomes very, very shaky. And at some point, yeah, something cracks. Anyway, Michael, thank you so much for taking the time.
Michael Hudson
We still have a little bit of time. You mentioned war with Russia. That’s really the key — how long will Russia, and Putin essentially, prevent the military in Russia from responding to the missile and drone attacks on its territory that are hitting its refineries and now hitting civilian targets, hitting Moscow and St. Petersburg, and the attempt by NATO to put more weapons in Finland and other Baltic countries? How long will Russia refrain from responding by doing what Putin had threatened to do — respond by bombing the factories that make the missiles that are bombing them, the factories in Germany or France or Britain that are providing the missiles? At some point, Russia is now realizing it’s not fighting against Ukraine. Ukraine is the arena for this fighting. The fight is with NATO. Ukraine just doesn’t matter. The Russian troops are moving westward in Ukraine. They’re moving toward taking over Odessa. They’re blocking Ukrainian access to Odessa and to export their own grain, sunflower oil, and other materials. But this doesn’t prevent the NATO countries from sending missiles from Ukraine into Russia. And the enemy isn’t really Ukraine any longer. It’s Germany, France, and Britain that are acting as U.S. satellites in attacking Russia and letting the United States’ plans — I think it’s in Wiesbaden and other cities — guide the missiles that are hitting Russia. Well, I think the fact that they’re doing that is one reason that Russia is in a tit-for-tat response, saying, all right, we’re going to help provide Iran, if it needs it, with satellite guidance for its bombs to fight you. So that’s the escalation that’s occurring. And this escalation is, if it really is existential on both sides, then it’s going to continue to be very destructive. And the collateral damage will be the world economy, the Asian economy, Africa, and the Global South that are not going to get the fertilizer, which is going to reduce their crops, their ability to feed themselves, and will essentially subject them to famine. This year, 2026, is going to be a world-historical year for the showdown, when the dynamics that we’ve been discussing all come together.
Glenn Diesen
Yeah, I was going to say, interesting times. Well, even if all these wars ended now, it’s hard to see it not being a food crisis this autumn. Well, anyway, as I was going to say, I always feel a bit wiser talking to you, so thank you so much for your time.
Michael Hudson
Well, thank you for having me on.

results.title: Mercor is embracing old-school Big Tech interview strategies that even Google and Microsoft are ditching
results.author: Shubhangi Goel
results.content:
Mercor's interview process is less vibe coding, more whiteboarding.
On an episode of the "20VC" podcast released on Saturday, Mercor's head of product, Osvald Nitski, said that the AI training company has moved away from take-home assignments that can be completed with AI.
"We'll do one round where we find out if the person is familiar with AI tools," he said. "We care a lot about being able to set up good experiments and understanding statistics, having good judgment, and then systems design as well," he said, referring to what is asked in whiteboarding sessions.
Whiteboard interviews, where candidates draw and explain their thinking process, became an industry gold standard in the 2010s and are part of standard technical interviews at companies like Google, Meta, and Microsoft.
On the podcast, Nitski, who joined the $10 billion startup last year, said that AI makes it very easy to "offload" a lot of decision-making.
"We want to make sure that people still have the ability to have good judgment and know what they're doing and not just, like, regurgitate what comes out of Claude," he said.
While Mercor uses AI to screen candidates for its talent marketplace, its full-time job interview process contradicts what most of Silicon Valley is increasingly adopting.
For one, work trials and take-home assessments, which Nitski said Mercor has moved away from, are quickly replacing traditional interviews, such as culture-fit screenings and whiteboarding sessions. AI coding startups like Lovable, Cursor, and Kilo say work experiments are a one-shot way to gauge whether someone has the technical and soft skills they want to see.
Mercor's low-AI interview strategy is also unique compared to peers.
Over the last few months, Business Insider reported that Big Tech companies such as Google, Microsoft-owned LinkedIn, and Cisco are changing their interview to allow candidates to use AI. Some tech startups are giving candidates full access to AI tools and coding assistants.
Emily Cohen, who heads people and operations at AI coding startup Cognition, said the company has changed its interview process to account for AI and vibe coding.
"I guess this is like asking a kid to take a math test without a calculator," she said about not allowing AI use in interviews. "For the bulk of building something similar to what you would do on the role, you can and should use AI tools."

Mercor has shifted its hiring strategy away from AI-assisted take-home assignments, opting instead for traditional whiteboarding sessions to better evaluate a candidate's fundamental judgment and technical problem-solving skills.

### Key Points
- Head of Product Osvald Nitski confirmed the $10 billion startup now prioritizes whiteboarding to test systems design, statistical knowledge, and experimental reasoning.
- The company aims to prevent candidates from relying on AI tools like Claude to generate work rather than demonstrating independent decision-making abilities.
- This approach contrasts with industry trends where companies like Google, Microsoft, and various AI startups are increasingly integrating AI tools into their interview processes.
- Many tech firms now favor work trials and "vibe coding" assessments to gauge how effectively candidates utilize AI coding assistants in real-world scenarios.

### Why it Matters
This shift highlights a growing debate in the tech industry regarding whether to embrace AI-assisted workflows or prioritize foundational human expertise during recruitment. By rejecting AI-heavy assessments, Mercor is positioning itself against the broader Silicon Valley trend of integrating generative tools into standard technical evaluations.

results.title: 5 Tiny Homes and Fold-Out Cabins Built to Move Wherever You Go
results.author: Pooja Khanna Tyagi
results.content:
Portable architecture is shifting how space, ownership, and mobility are defined. What once existed as temporary or emergency structures now evolves into refined, design-led systems that move with the user. Compact cabins and adaptable living units reflect a growing demand for flexibility while maintaining comfort, function, and a strong sense of identity.
A clear transition is visible from static buildings toward environments that can expand, relocate, and adjust over time. This evolution aligns with changing lifestyles where mobility, efficiency, and intentional living shape how spaces are experienced. The result is a new architectural language where structures are no longer fixed, but responsive and continuously adaptable.
1. Fold-Out Cabins with Compact Design That Expands on Demand
Fold-out cabins transform the way space is utilized by shifting from compact units into fully functional living environments within minutes. Designed for flexibility, they can be transported and deployed wherever required, making them suitable for remote work, short-term retreats, or temporary housing. Smart layouts integrate sleeping, cooking, and storage within a minimal footprint, ensuring efficiency without compromising comfort.
Their appeal lies in balancing mobility with a sense of permanence. These structures can be placed in natural landscapes, urban backyards, or transitional sites, creating continuity between movement and stability. For Gen Z and minimal living approaches, they reflect a lifestyle that prioritizes flexibility, purpose, and essential comfort.
The modern world is increasingly shaped by overlapping crises such as climate change, displacement, and large-scale emergencies, pushing architects to rethink how shelter can be delivered quickly and effectively. In this context, Hariri & Hariri, a New York–based architecture practice founded by Gisue and Mojgan Hariri, developed a prefabricated folding cabin designed to provide immediate, functional housing without the need for tools, hardware, or manual assembly.
Inspired by origami, the cabin is engineered as a compact folded structure that can be transported efficiently on flatbed trucks. Once placed on site, it unfolds into a fully formed modular unit, expanding rapidly into a single-story living space. The design emphasizes speed and autonomy, allowing the structure to self-deploy when activated, which is especially critical in emergency conditions where time and resources are limited. Lightweight materials such as glass and Equitone panels ensure portability while maintaining durability and usability across diverse environments and needs.
2. Portable Saunas for Recreation and Wellness on the Move
Portable saunas shift the focus from living to recreation by bringing wellness into flexible, transportable formats. These compact units allow users to create a sauna experience wherever they choose, from outdoor settings to travel destinations, without relying on permanent installations. Designed for ease of setup and use, they make relaxation and recovery more accessible in changing environments.
This evolution highlights how portable architecture is extending into lifestyle and leisure. It is not about redefining home, but about enhancing moments of pause and restoration. By integrating heat therapy into mobile setups, portable saunas support a routine centered on well-being, adaptability, and everyday recreation.
For those who enjoy saunas, the idea of a semi-portable structure that can be transported, assembled, and disassembled across different terrains offers a new way to experience relaxation in nature. Instead of being tied to a fixed location, this concept allows wellness spaces to move with the user, opening possibilities for retreats in forests, mountains, or coastal landscapes. Designed by BIVAK Studio, the SAUNABIVAK explores this idea through a prefabricated, transportable sauna system intended for ease of setup and mobility.
The structure features a double-layer glass wall that preserves views of the surrounding environment while maintaining insulation. It is built using cross-laminated timber panels for strength and lightness, supported on four legs that eliminate the need for permanent foundations. Treated with linseed oil for durability, it is weather-resistant and insect-protected, with natural ventilation and a firewood heating system inside. Designed within European towing limits, it can be installed by two people in about an hour, making it a practical blend of mobility, simplicity, and immersive outdoor wellness.
3. Micro Offices That Redefine Work Beyond Fixed Spaces
Micro offices respond to evolving work culture by offering compact, transportable environments designed for focus and flexibility. These units can be placed in a range of settings, providing a private workspace without the need for long-term leases or permanent infrastructure. Their efficient design supports daily productivity while adapting to changing professional needs.
They enable greater control over how and where work happens while maintaining mobility. Positioned in gardens, rooftops, or shared environments, micro offices challenge traditional office models by removing fixed spatial limits and supporting a more adaptable, self-directed way of working.
The rise of micro offices has introduced a new way of thinking about workspaces, focusing on compact, flexible environments that support concentration and privacy. In this context, Make.Work.Space presents itself as a personal work pod designed to function as a private productivity zone. It can be installed in homes, corporate offices, or even public environments, adapting easily to different spatial needs while improving efficiency and comfort.
The system is available in three modular versions: Micro-Office 1, 2, and 3, each designed for varying levels of use and comfort. The most compact model includes essential features such as a fixed desk, acoustic paneling, lighting, and built-in power access. The larger versions expand functionality with ergonomic tables, panoramic windows, ventilation systems, and optional air conditioning. Across all versions, the design prioritizes privacy, focus, and adaptability, while also making better use of underutilized spaces. Make.Work.Space offers a flexible solution for modern working, resting, or retreating within limited environments.
4. Houses on Wheels Enabling Fully Mobile Living
Houses on wheels merge the idea of home with continuous mobility, creating self-contained living systems designed for travel. Unlike temporary shelters, they support long-term habitation, often incorporating kitchens, bathrooms, and sleeping areas within a compact structure. This integration allows everyday living to function seamlessly while on the move.
They appeal to those seeking to move beyond fixed living patterns without losing a sense of stability. Relocation becomes part of routine life, not a disruption, allowing continuity across changing locations while maintaining comfort, familiarity, and independence.
Tiny House du Lac by Plume is designed within the constraints of France’s strict towing regulations, which often result in more compact and highly efficient mobile homes. At just 17.8 feet in length, the structure prioritizes portability while still accommodating up to two people comfortably, or a small family of three in a more tightly arranged layout. The design reflects a clear focus on minimal footprint and mobility without sacrificing essential living functions.
Inside, the layout is defined by a single continuous space that maximizes every inch of the interior. The kitchen is compact yet fully equipped with essential fittings, while the adjacent living area includes a small sofa and a fold-down dining table, maintaining a sense of openness through light tones and wooden finishes. At the opposite end, the bedroom is designed as a loft-style sleeping area accessed by wooden steps, with the space beneath adapted for storage or additional use.
5. Towable Stores Bringing Retail Directly to Changing Locations
Towable stores place commerce in motion by enabling businesses to operate through mobile retail units. These setups can be moved across locations, events, or neighborhoods, allowing brands to engage directly with audiences without depending on fixed storefronts. Their compact and adaptable design supports quick deployment and efficient operation in varied settings.
This approach encourages flexibility and experimentation within retail. Businesses can test new markets, respond to shifting demand, and create immediate, location-driven shopping experiences. It redefines how products are presented and accessed, making retail more responsive, mobile, and connected to its audience.
SHOPKIT, designed by Japanese studio COC, is a modular mobile store system created for easy setup, transport, and reuse in different environments. It functions as a compact retail unit that can be quickly assembled and disassembled, making it suitable for events, exhibitions, trade fairs, or temporary shop installations. Built with materials like wood, steel, and polycarbonate, the structure maintains a clean, minimal design while remaining durable and adaptable across various urban and outdoor settings.
The system is available in two configurations: a single-door version and a larger double-door version. The single-door unit offers a simple, compact retail setup, while the double-door option expands into a more functional store layout with counters, translucent panels for natural lighting, and space for display and interaction. Designed to be portable and efficient, SHOPKIT transforms temporary retail needs into a structured mobile shop that can be placed wherever selling space is required.
Portable architecture reflects a shift toward flexible, mobile living where spaces adapt to changing needs. It spans living, work, and recreation, rethinking how environments function and respond to users. Mobility, efficiency, and intentional use become central to contemporary design, replacing fixed and static spatial models.
results.summary:
Portable architecture is transforming modern living and commerce by replacing static buildings with adaptable, mobile structures designed for rapid deployment, efficient space utilization, and increased user flexibility.

### Key Points
- Hariri & Hariri developed an origami-inspired, prefabricated folding cabin that deploys without tools for emergency or remote housing.
- BIVAK Studio’s SAUNABIVAK is a transportable, cross-laminated timber sauna designed for two-person assembly in under one hour.
- Make.Work.Space offers three modular micro-office versions featuring acoustic paneling and ergonomic designs to facilitate private, flexible work environments.
- Plume’s Tiny House du Lac is a 17.8-foot mobile home built to meet strict French towing regulations while housing up to three people.
- The COC-designed SHOPKIT provides a modular, mobile retail system made of wood and steel for temporary storefronts and event-based commerce.

### Why it Matters
This shift toward portable architecture reflects a broader move away from permanent, fixed-location infrastructure in favor of responsive, high-efficiency design. By prioritizing mobility and modularity, these innovations offer practical solutions for housing crises, remote work trends, and the growing demand for flexible, intentional living spaces.

results.title: 'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
results.author: Abhik Deb
results.content:
'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct.
In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests".
Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit.
Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years".
On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times.
Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram."
The latest education protests erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal.
The outrage was channelled by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online campaign launched after India's chief justice likened unemployed people with "fake and bogus degrees" to cockroaches. Its founders staged a sit-in in Delhi, demanding Pradhan's resignation, education reforms and compensation for the bereaved families.
Two days later, tens of thousands marched on parliament at the CJP's call, triggering a police crackdown. Videos of baton charges, tear gas and pellet guns spread rapidly online, fuelling public anger and swelling the protests instead of suppressing them.
The discontent among India's youth and the courage to voice it on the streets spread to other parts of the country.
Somaya Korde was detained at home after urging people online to join a 20 July protest in Mumbai, but went on to attend multiple demonstrations in the days that followed.
Pradhan's resignation, says the 26-year-old, "is not the end, but just the beginning".
"For this generation, this is the first time many of us have stepped out to protest. But there are larger issues to talk about, and we will talk about them," she says.
Korde, the first woman in her family to graduate in law and a recent civic election candidate, comes from a community officially classified as "backward" because of its historic social and economic disadvantage.
Like many young Indians, she saw education as her path to a better life, but says the NEET paper leak shattered her faith in a system that promised hard work would be rewarded.
"Schools and colleges are being privatised, paper leaks are happening, even if you finish education, there are not enough jobs. In a democracy, all this raises questions of accountability against the government," she says.
Her frustration is indicative of a larger picture.
India has the world's largest youth population, yet unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in June from 13.8% a year earlier, according to government data.
The protests became a rallying point for young people to shed their caution and voice their frustration. Among them was 18-year-old Harshvardhan Kadam, who took a part-time job selling laptops after finishing school to help support his mother following his father's death last year.
On 23 July, a video Harshvardhan filmed during a protest march in Mumbai went viral. In the Instagram reel, now viewed 10 million times, a policeman is seen threatening to frame him in a fake drugs case while detaining him in a police van. The constable has since been suspended.
"I did not wish him to be suspended," Kadam told the BBC, "I just wanted to document how the police were treating me for participating in a peaceful protest." Now, reflecting on Pradhan's resignation he says: "This is just the start. This shows that next time the government will be scared when we raise our voices."
Swaraj Priyo, a 29-year-old screenwriter from Guwahati, says years of protesting under the Modi government had left him disillusioned by the lack of change. But this movement, he says, has restored hope: "This movement has brought back space for question and dissent and the reality check that all is not over."
A growing sense that the Modi government is on the back foot is palpable. Protest sites across the country now display posters declaring: "Pradhan was just an example. It's Modi's turn next".
But alongside this bullishness comes some apprehension.
Varuni Poorva, a 30-year-old aspiring professor from Patna and a student activist for nearly a decade, says Pradhan's resignation shows the Modi government can be "brought to its knees".
But she fears a "witch hunt" against protesters despite the government's pledge not to act against those who organised or joined the demonstrations.
Over the past week, she has sought anticipatory bail to guard against possible arrest. Police have charged more than 100 protesters with offences including attempted murder, and arrested more than 40.
Despite fears of a crackdown, shared by many students' parents, Poorva believes the protests have given young people newfound confidence. With their deeper frustrations unresolved, she says, it will be difficult for the government to return to "business as usual".
At one protest site in Delhi, graffiti captures the mood: "We do not have jobs. If you wipe this out, we will come back tomorrow".
results.summary:
India’s youth-led protest movement successfully forced the resignation of a cabinet minister following a major medical exam scandal, signaling a shift in political accountability under Prime Minister Modi.

### Key Points
- Education Minister Pradhan resigned after the NEET medical entrance exam was cancelled due to a widespread question paper leak affecting two million students.
- The Cockroach Janta Party, an online activist group, organized nationwide demonstrations that utilized Instagram to bypass mainstream media narratives.
- Government data shows unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 rose to 16.2% in June, fueling deep-seated frustration regarding job prospects and systemic corruption.
- Police responded to protests with baton charges and mass detentions, leading to over 40 arrests and charges of attempted murder against demonstrators.
- Viral social media documentation of police misconduct, including a widely viewed video in Mumbai, has bolstered public support for the student-led movement.

### Why it Matters
This movement represents a rare instance of organized dissent challenging the current administration's long-standing political dominance. It highlights the growing influence of digital-native youth in shaping national discourse and demanding accountability for systemic failures in education and employment.

results.title: AppleCare One launching in the UK as theft and loss coverage expands
results.author: Ben Lovejoy
results.content:
AppleCare One – a version of AppleCare+ that allows you to protect multiple products for a single monthly payment – is rolling out the the UK.
Additionally, AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss protection is also expanding from iPhone only to iPad and Apple Watch too …
Standard AppleCare+ covers accidental damage as well as product failure outside of warranty, while the more comprehensive option of AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss has only been available for iPhone in the UK. You’ll now be able to choose this plan for iPad and Apple Watch also.
Additionally, if you want full coverage for three or more Apple products, you can opt instead for AppleCare One, which will be cheaper than individual plans.
AppleCare One costs £16.99 per month for three products, and additional devices can be added for £4.99/month each. It will be available from tomorrow.
If you currently have an AppleCare+ plan for one or more products, you’ll be able to seamlessly transition them to AppleCare One, even if you bought an annual plan. Adding a product to AppleCare One will automatically cancel its existing AppleCare+ plan, and Apple will refund any unused portion. Similarly, if you use Apple trade-in to upgrade any product on your plan, coverage will transfer between devices automatically.
In most cases, you’ll be able to sign up on your device or on apple.com. You may be required to verify the condition of your device, but this too can usually be done from your own home, running a diagnostic and taking photos. This requirement is waived if you already have AppleCare+ coverage or purchased very recently. Only in exceptional cases will you need to visit an Apple store.
There is some small-print you need to be aware of. First, existing devices must be no more than four years old at the point of enrolment (one year for headphones), and must be registered in your Apple account. For AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss, you get unlimited accidental damage claims, while theft and loss claims max out at two per year. For AppleCare One, you get a total of three claims per year across all devices.
If you do need to make a claim, the following excess fees apply per device:
- iPhone: £109
- iPad: £99
- Watch: £89
- MacBook Neo: $49 for screen or enclosure, $149 for anything else
- All other Macs: $99 for screen or enclosure, $299 for anything else

Apple is launching AppleCare One in the UK, a subscription service allowing users to bundle protection for multiple devices under a single monthly payment starting at £16.99.

### Key Points
- AppleCare One covers three devices for £16.99 monthly, with additional products added for £4.99 each.
- Theft and Loss protection is expanding in the UK to include iPad and Apple Watch models.

It also provides UK users with broader access to theft and loss coverage, potentially increasing long-term hardware retention and service revenue for the company.

What you need to know
- Google is developing a new "Phone to Watch Unlock" feature that automatically unlocks your Pixel Watch with your Pixel phone.
- The feature works in reverse of today's Watch Unlock, eliminating the need to enter your watch PIN repeatedly.
- Code strings suggest the feature will be exclusive to the Pixel Watch and Pixel phone ecosystem through Connected Services.
Google could finally fix the one thing that's been annoying me about using a passcode on my Pixel Watch.
For quite some time now, Google has offered a feature called Watch Unlock that lets your Pixel Watch unlock your Pixel phone. If your Pixel Watch is already unlocked and on your wrist, your phone automatically unlocks without asking for your passcode. The problem is that it doesn't work the other way around.
Thankfully, that could finally be changing.
As spotted by Android Authority, Google is working on a new feature called Phone to Watch Unlock that would automatically unlock your Pixel Watch whenever you unlock your paired Pixel phone.
Unlike the current implementation, where an unlocked Pixel Watch can unlock your phone, this feature would work in reverse. Once you unlock your Pixel phone, your Pixel Watch will automatically unlock as well. It's something that's been bugging me for a long time, so I'm glad to see Google finally working on a fix.
Unfortunately, it looks like this feature will be exclusive to the Pixel ecosystem. The code strings were discovered in Google's Connected Phone and Watch Services app, suggesting it will only work between Pixel phones and Pixel Watches.
From what it appears, Google will prompt users to enable the feature during setup. You'll first need to enter your current watch PIN as a one-time verification, after which your Pixel Watch will automatically unlock whenever you unlock your Pixel phone.

results.title: NASA Replaces ULA's Vulcan Centaur With SpaceX Falcon Heavy For Solar Storm Research
results.author: EditorDavid
results.content:
There's been a change to NASA's launch of six satellites for solar storms research.   Space.com reports that those satellites "were originally slated to lift off on a United Launch Alliance Vulcan Centaur rocket but have now been assigned a SpaceX Falcon Heavy, according to a NASA mission update."
[NASA's Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment mision — or SunRISE] will fly to space as part of a rideshare mission sponsored by the U.S. Space Force's Space Systems Command. NASA has reassigned its SunRISE solar research mission from a United Launch Alliance Vulcan Centaur rocket to a SpaceX Falcon Heavy following recent booster anomalies during national security launches.

### Key Points
- NASA’s Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment (SunRISE) consists of six satellites designed to study solar storms and improve space weather prediction models.
- The mission was moved to a SpaceX Falcon Heavy after the U.S. Space Force paused Vulcan Centaur launches due to recurring solid rocket booster issues.
- Vulcan Centaur experienced anomalies during two of its four total flights, including the recent USSF-87 national security mission.
- SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy has successfully completed 12 launches since 2018, including four missions carrying national security payloads.
- The SunRISE mission is currently scheduled to launch later this year as part of a rideshare program managed by the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command.

### Why it Matters
This shift highlights the critical role of launch vehicle reliability in maintaining the schedule for essential government and scientific space missions. By moving to the proven Falcon Heavy platform, NASA ensures that vital solar research continues without further delays caused by ongoing technical investigations into the Vulcan rocket.
