results.title: CLARITY hopes fade, BitMEX shuts as lawsuit looms: Hodler’s Digest, July 26
results.author: Cointelegraph by Andrew Fenton
results.content:
CLARITY hopes fade, BitMEX shuts as lawsuit looms: Hodler’s Digest, July 26
Despite support from Goldman Sachs, Fidelity and law enforcement bodies, the Clarity Act’s chances dim. BitMEX to close as crypto consolidates into five big players.
CLARITY may get a vote, but don’t get your hopes up yet
Despite wealthy memecoin entrepreneur President Donald Trump agreeing to an ethics deal, the Clarity Act (CLARITY) is floundering as the August recess deadline looms.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he doesn’t believe the act has the votes to pass just yet, but may bring it to a vote anyway to “get Clarity started. We’ll see where the votes are.”
The ethics deal would prohibit all US officials from issuing or sponsoring digital assets, but contains some “get out of jail free” provisions for the President that the Democrats are unhappy with, including the fact the rules expire the day he is scheduled to leave office in 2029.
The ethics provisions will also be enforced by the Attorney General that Trump appointed. The Democrats instead want state Attorney Generals to enforce it — but Trump seems unlikely to agree to empower dozens of state AGs to attempt to prosecute him.
The White House described the bill as the “most comprehensive and wide-ranging ethics provision in history,” while Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego described it as a “piece of s---” and “not a serious effort.”
Negotiations are continuing to find a deal both sides can live with, but given the lack of trust, it’s not going to be easy to find a compromise. 
Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon conceded the bill is “not perfect” but has supported it anyway, along with Fidelity and Charles Schwab who represent many trillions in assets under management each. 
Law enforcement organizations have also begun to signal support, with The National Fraternal Order of Police representing hundreds of thousands of members, stating the latest version of the BRCA (which protects developers of decentralized protocols) would not impede investigations into money laundering and fraud.
The odds of the bill passing this year are at 38% on Polymarket.
BitMEX to shut down after 11 years as class action launched against it
BitMEX, one of the pioneers of cryptocurrency derivatives trading, announced it will shut down operations in September after 11 years.
BitMEX launched in 2014 and became known for introducing the 100x leverage perpetual swaps.
In recent years volumes have tanked increased competition from major exchanges like Binance and decentralized protocols like Hyperliquid. 
CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju said BitMEX’s share of the Bitcoin futures market has fallen to just 0.08%, with roughly $84 million in daily trading volume.
“It was a great exchange that helped shape the industry, and now it is passing the torch to the next generation of exchanges it inspired,” Ju said.
BitMEX’s utility token BMEX collapsed in value after the announcement. That same day, news emerged of a class action lawsuit accusing the crypto derivatives platform of fraudulently engineering customer liquidations to seize traders’ collateral. BitMEX denied the allegations and said it had successfully defended itself against similar claims in the past.
Restructuring adviser Roshan Dharia told Cointelegraph the exchange’s demise shows the industry is consolidating.
The top five platforms now control an estimated 80% of global spot volume, leaving mid-tier and regional exchanges with shrinking margins and no viable path to scale... The headwinds are structural, not cyclical.
As if to undescore the point, BitMart subsequently announced it would also close in the coming months.
S&P launches blockchain fundamentals index for digital assets
S&P Dow Jones Indices and Pantera Capital have launched a digital asset index that tracks the major crypto assets — but doesn’t include Bitcoin or XRP.
The S&P Pantera Digital Asset Index is designed to be the benchmark crypto index for institutions, but it screens out blockchains based on minimum thresholds for protocol revenue, market capitalization and liquidity.
The index launched with 18 constituents, with Ether (ETH), BNB (BNB), Solana (SOL), TRON (TRX) and Hyperliquid (HYPE) as its five largest holdings, while Bitcoin (BTC) and XRP (XRP) are the largest non-constituents.
The latest index follows a broader industry push to develop institutional-grade benchmarks for digital assets, with similar products including the Nasdaq Crypto Index US ETF, the Franklin Crypto Index ETF and the the Coinbase Store of Value Index among others.
Robinhood to expand prediction markets as CFTC issues new warning
Robinhood is reportedly discussing plans to expand its existing prediction markets offerings with crypto exchange Crypto.com.
According the Wall Street Journal the talks involve integrating yes-or-no event contracts supplied by Crypto.com. Robinhood launched its prediction markets in March 2025, initially facilitated by Kalshi in order to comply with regulatory requirements from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). 
Bernstein analysts last week raised its price target on Robinhood (HOOD) stock to $160 from $130 per share, based on the company’s outlook for prediction markets and tokenized equities.
Meanwhile the CFTC, which aims to become the primary regulator of prediction markets, issued a shot across the bow of providers last week, telling platforms they need to get a lot more specific about event contracts certifications.
The advisory addresses concerns about the practice of submitting broad, template-style certifications that combine many potential event contract variations into a single certification.
Carl Kennedy, a partner at New York law firm Katten Muchin, also told a House Agriculture Committee hearing last week, that the CLARITY Act could help the CFTC’s efforts to oversee the “explosive growth of prediction markets.”
Balaji’s Network School turns to Kazakhstan amid Malaysia setback
Balaji Srinivasan’s Network School, a community of “digital nomads,” is eyeing a new campus in Kazakhstan after its Forest City campus had its business license in Malaysia revoked over alleged premises-use violations.
A memorandum of understanding was signed between Kazakhstan’s relevant Minister Zhaslan Madiyev and Srinivasan to establish the first Network School campus in the country, which aims to become a digital hub.
The school was forced out of Johor in Malaysia, following a controversy in Malaysia over allowing Israeli dual citizens to attend. The Muslim majority country has no diplomatic relations with Israel. Despite an investigation finding no visa violations, the Network School was ordered to shut down on another pretext.
Dragonfly Capital managing partner Haseeb Qureshi said the drama has validated Balaji’s Network State thesis.
“The whole idea of a network state is taking a dense group of talent and capital, and collectively negotiating with states. The Malaysia drama set up Balaji to negotiate better terms with another state to copy and paste the network there.“
Winners and losers
At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is at $65,395, Ether (ETH) is at $1,958, and XRP (XRP) is at $1.11. The total market cap is at $2.24 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.
Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Audiera (BEAT), which gained 53%,  Shinba Inu (SHIB) with a 29% gain, and Venice Token (VVV), which increased 19%.
The top three altcoin losers of the week are DeXe (DEXE), which lost 89%, Midnight (NIGHT), which fell 26%, and Pyth Network (PYTH), which dropped 10%.
Prediction of the Week
Bitcoin will get ‘lift’ from Hyperliquid, Robinhood in next crypto bull market
Bitcoin (BTC) is “finally showing signs of a bottom,” according to Matt Hougan, chief investment officer at Bitwise.
Houghan predicts that TradFi integrations, particularly Hyperliquid and Robinhood, will drive the next crypto bull market, and the resulting tide should “lift” the largest cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin and Ether.
Houghan believes crypto is bringing major benefits like 24/7 trading to traditional markets, and noted that today “nearly half the volume on Hyperliquid is in conventional assets like oil, silver, and the S&P 500 [and] it’s expanding into spot commodities, prediction markets, and options,”
Bitwise data also suggests apparent demand for BTC is showing signs of reversal. The metric measures the difference between newly-mined BTC and the supply inactive for at least one year. 
Top FUD of the Week
Home invasions became most common crypto wrench attack in H1 2026: CertiK
Home invasions became the most common form of crypto wrench attacks during the first half of 2026, rising to 20 publicly reported incidents from just one a year earlier, according to blockchain security firm CertiK.
On Thursday, CertiK said it verified 52 wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up 33.3% from 39 incidents during the same period in 2025. Kidnappings rose to 16 from 12, while robberies declined from five incidents to one.
CertiK said the recorded financial exposure linked to the attacks reached about $124.1 million, up from $10.5 million a year earlier.
The increase in home invasions suggests criminals are increasingly bypassing digital safeguards by physically coercing crypto holders and their families.
Hackers steal $31.6M in 2 crypto bridge attacks within 7 hours
Hackers stole more than $31.6 million across two unrelated crypto bridge exploits spaced just hours apart, targeting bridges operated by decentralized perpetual exchange AFX and Verus Protocol.
According to Blockaid, AFX, a decentralized perpetual exchange operating on Arbitrum, reportedly lost $24.15 million on Wednesday through a hack targeting one of its cross-chain bridges. Hours later, Blockaid said it detected an exploit targeting the Verus Ethereum Bridge that resulted in about $7.5 million in crypto being stolen.
“Another bridge, another exploit. Bridges will always be a weak link, until security is upgraded,” onchain investigator TheCrypticWolf said in a post on X.
Ethereum ETFs close week in red, end 5-day inflow streak
US-listed spot Ethereum exchange-traded funds (ETFs) logged $70.62 million in net outflows on Friday, ending a five-day inflow streak.
Ethereum funds saw $211.25 million in net inflows over the previous five sessions from July 17, according to SoSoValue data. They still posted $103.9 million in net inflows for the week ended Friday.
Despite the outflows, Ethereum ETFs extended their weekly inflow streak to three straight and have attracted $337.74 million in net inflows so far in July.
The Bitcoin ETFs reversed gains made earlier in the week to end up with $33.9 million of inflows. 
Top Magazine Stories of the Week
Both parties say they want US crypto market structure legislation, but a dispute over ethics rules and who enforces them is becoming the bill’s biggest obstacle.
A Bitcoin development roadmap that addresses quantum computing risks could see the price surge by “double digits” very quickly, according to Charles Edwards.
Are the fears of an AI driven hacking epidemic totally overblown, or is this just the lull before the storm?
results.summary:
The Clarity Act faces legislative uncertainty as BitMEX prepares to shut down, highlighting a broader trend of market consolidation and regulatory challenges across the cryptocurrency industry this week.

### Key Points
- The Clarity Act faces dimming prospects as Senate Majority Leader John Thune questions whether the bill has sufficient support to pass before the August recess.
- BitMEX will cease operations in September after 11 years, as the exchange faces a class action lawsuit and declining market share against larger competitors.
- S&P Dow Jones Indices launched a new digital asset index featuring 18 constituents, notably excluding Bitcoin and XRP in favor of assets like Ether and Solana.
- CertiK reported that crypto-related home invasions surged to 20 incidents in the first half of 2026, with total financial losses from physical "wrench attacks" reaching $124.1 million.
- Hackers stole $31.6 million in two separate bridge exploits targeting the AFX exchange and Verus Protocol within a seven-hour window.

### Why it Matters
The simultaneous struggle of legislative reform and the exit of legacy exchanges like BitMEX signal a structural shift toward a more consolidated, institutional-grade crypto market. As mid-tier platforms struggle to compete, the industry is increasingly defined by regulatory scrutiny and the need for robust security standards to protect against rising physical and digital threats.

results.title: Space Data Centers Proposed by Big Tech Could Be “Catastrophic,” Experts Warn in FCC Petition
results.author: Iva Greene
results.content:
The petition – submitted by Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility, Earthjustice and DarkSky International – argues that deploying millions of satellites to create orbital data centers would release staggering levels of pollution likely to alter Earth's atmosphere and be "catastrophic" for the planet, according to experts cited in the document. The petition states that the companies have collectively proposed fleets of thousands of satellites, but have refused to embrace any inquiry into the environmental impacts of their plans.
"These same proponents have refused to embrace any inquiry into the impacts of their self-claimed epochal technology on the environment, science, economy or other values," the petition reads, according to a report by The Guardian. The groups urge the FCC to assess the environmental consequences before granting any new licenses, warning that the cumulative harms from more than a million satellites orbiting, colliding and disintegrating back to Earth remain unexamined.
Satellites and rockets release a range of pollutants during launch and when they burn up upon re-entry, including black soot, aluminum oxides, rare metals, and other toxic substances. According to a 2023 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)-sponsored stratospheric measurement flight reported by The Guardian, scientists detected metals from spacecraft in sulfuric acid aerosols in the stratosphere, a highly sensitive atmospheric layer.
The interaction between these spacecraft metals, naturally occurring metals, and sulfuric acid aerosols is described as "largely unknown" by the researchers behind the study. These pollutants are accumulating in the stratosphere at alarming levels, according to the petition. Rocket launches alone emit black carbon, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, aluminum oxide, chlorine gases and mercury, as detailed by experts.
A separate report on rocket fuel pollution noted that toxic chemicals from rocket launches can spread across large areas, as demonstrated by a Chinese rocket fuel dump that affected seven U.S. states in 2025, adding to the chemical chaos from atmospheric spraying, according to NaturalNews.com [1]. The petition argues that the cumulative effect of millions of satellites, each decommissioned and incinerated after five to 15 years, would inject unprecedented quantities of pollutants into the pristine upper atmosphere.
Some scientists fear the accumulation of these pollutants could destroy the ozone layer, potentially exposing people to higher levels of harmful ultraviolet radiation, and further destabilize the climate. The stratospheric aerosols that contain the spacecraft metals normally play a role in regulating Earth’s temperature by reflecting solar radiation and preventing greenhouse gases from entering the ozone layer from below.
However, the impact of the added metals on this process remains uncertain, according to the NOAA study cited in the petition. Light pollution from millions of satellites would also permanently transform the night sky, according to advocates. "These projects could permanently alter the night sky as we know it," said Ruskin Hartley, executive director of DarkSky International, in comments reported by The Guardian.
Astronomers have long warned about increasing light pollution from satellite megaconstellations, which they say obscures astronomical observations and harms wildlife that depend on natural darkness, as noted in reports about technology pollution threatening astronomy [2] and calls for governments to intervene on satellite proliferation [3]. Hartley said the FCC must take seriously its obligation to ensure these projects do not cause unnecessary harm to naturally dark skies.
Several former federal space officials expressed doubts about the feasibility of orbital data centers, while also warning of the environmental risks. Steve Volz, the former head of NOAA's satellite office, told The Guardian: "There is a lot of complex material in these things, and even if they do burn up, you do not want to be filling up the atmosphere with refuse from these any more than you would want it coming from a smoke stack."
Cole Donovan, a former NOAA space policy expert now with Stand Up for Science, noted that the space data centers would demand a huge amount of rare metals and other resources already in short supply. This, in turn, would create additional environmental challenges on the ground.
The petition cites the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), arguing that federal agencies are required to assess the environmental impacts of proposed projects. It states that FCC applications from companies such as Cowboy Space Corporation and SpaceX fail to address these risks.
According to the petition, Cowboy Space's only reference to environmental mitigation is a promise to minimize impact on astronomy, while SpaceX claims its data centers will "ensur[e] humanity’s multi-planetary future amongst the stars" but offers no detail on environmental protections, beyond a vague promise of "industry-leading brightness mitigations." The petition argues that no proponent has provided satisfactory detail on mitigating cumulative harm from millions of satellites.
The massive investment in data centers on Earth is already straining energy and water resources, with trillions of dollars committed to construction globally, consuming millions of kilowatts of electricity and large amounts of land and water, as noted in discussions about the scale of data center growth [4].
The petition submits that the FCC is legally required to determine whether granting satellite licenses serves the public interest, convenience, and necessity, and that the NEPA provides mechanisms to assess impacts, examine alternatives and disclose risks. The groups urge the commission to pause all new licenses for space data center projects until a thorough environmental review is completed.
"No proponent has provided satisfactory detail to explain how it will mitigate the cumulative environmental harms flowing from the foreseeable operation of more than a million satellites, orbiting our planet, colliding and disintegrating and plummeting back to Earth," the petition states, as quoted by The Guardian. Without such an assessment, the groups warn, the consequences of moving data centers into space could be catastrophic for the Earth's atmosphere, ozone layer and night sky, while also diverting resources from more sustainable terrestrial alternatives.
results.summary:
Environmental advocacy groups have petitioned the FCC to halt satellite licensing, citing concerns that orbital data centers could cause catastrophic atmospheric pollution and permanent damage to the night sky.

### Key Points
- Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility, Earthjustice, and DarkSky International filed the petition to mandate environmental reviews for satellite megaconstellations.
- The petition warns that millions of satellites burning up upon re-entry release toxic metals and pollutants into the stratosphere, potentially damaging the ozone layer.
- NOAA-sponsored research has already detected spacecraft-derived metals within sensitive stratospheric aerosols, though the long-term climate impacts remain largely unknown.
- Critics argue that companies like SpaceX and Cowboy Space Corporation have failed to provide adequate environmental mitigation plans for their proposed orbital infrastructure.
- The groups invoke the National Environmental Policy Act, asserting the FCC must assess cumulative environmental risks before granting further satellite deployment licenses.

### Why it Matters
This petition highlights a growing conflict between the rapid expansion of space-based technology and the preservation of Earth's atmospheric and astronomical integrity. If successful, the request could force a significant regulatory shift, requiring tech companies to prove their projects are environmentally sustainable before receiving federal approval.

results.title: I rebuilt my home servers from scratch, and this is the OS setup I wish I'd started with
results.author: Rich Edmonds
results.content:
When I set up my first home server, I won't lie and say it was Proxmox. It was Ubuntu Server, something I had extensive history and experience using. I eventually ended up on Proxmox, but the journey here could have been skipped entirely if I had started with the Linux-based hypervisor from the get-go. I recently rebuilt my home lab from scratch, and Proxmox was front and center, creating the ultimate home-based data center.
Proxmox offers the best of both worlds
It's great for self-hosting and data storage
Prior to trying Proxmox, I would always view a server and as two completely separate elements. They only shared internal parts, as the software running on them and the tasks handled were vastly different. That's not the case with Proxmox. This may be a hypervisor, but that allows the platform to be used for just about everything within the home lab. Need a NAS? Proxmox can handle it. Self-hosting? That too. It's very versatile.
But even if you choose not to use Proxmox for everything, it's now the default OS for my servers. TrueNAS happily chugs away with countless terabytes of storage available across the entire network, but it's Proxmox that brings everything together with self-hosted apps. Using Debian, Ubuntu Server, FreeBSD, or some other flavor of Unix allows for some powerful servers to be created. It's much easier to go from nothing to a bustling home lab with Docker containers.
That's where cracks can start to appear. For instance, when I first launched one of my home-based servers with Ubuntu Server, there wasn't really a way to manage it remotely with a functional web UI. I couldn't simply load up a URL in the browser on any device connected to the network. SSH is perfectly serviceable, but sometimes I don't want to work in access or bother running long commands on a touch screen. I wanted something a little easier to use.
Even if you happen to be an absolute Linux beginner and are looking to move away from using prebuilt NAS enclosures or wish to supplement one with a slightly more capable system, Proxmox is still the way to go.
It's surprisingly easy to learn and use
You'll go from zero to hero in no time
Proxmox isn't anywhere close to as daunting as it may seem initially. Sure, the installation process may not be as refined as Windows, macOS, or even Synology's DSM, but it doesn't need to be. This is going to be the only time you see it with a single home server. I've only had to reinstall Proxmox once, and that's because I did something really dumb. That's the beauty of Proxmox. It's an underlying system for other OS installs and software to run on top of.
If you're in the camp for wanting to learn more about Linux and virtualization, wish to consolidate self-hosted services, want to get into some cool technology like Pi-hole, and fancy yourself some experimentation, Proxmox is one of the best solutions. I currently have a cluster of three nodes. Two of these are almost identical with an Intel Core i5-7400 CPU, and the third is a Minisforum U850 with a Core i5-10210U.
These aren't powerful systems by any stretch, especially given I tried running my entire home lab on a single server with a 64-core AMD Ryzen Threadripper, but they're also incredibly friendly to my renewable energy installation and monthly utility bill. I can have everything runng — and by everything, I mean all services and a NAS storing all data — all for just north of $1 per day. That's around $37 per month and $450 each year.
It's all about the savings (no, seriously)
Compare that to a Netflix subscription, the cheapest starting from $9 per month. This one service costs more than $100 each year. There's a good chance you have multiple streaming services up and running, not to mention cloud storage and maybe even Microsoft Office. All this adds up and likely surpasses the amount I'm paying for a fully packed NAS and three Proxmox nodes running my entire home lab and smart home.
If you're wanting to maximize savings, this could be achieved by using a single prebuilt NAS or custom build with an OS that supports containers. Another way is to use Proxmox to run TrueNAS or some other NAS software in an isolated instance alongside all your services. That's the beauty of Proxmox and the wider home lab ... it's so flexible and can adjust to personal requirements. Being able to fire up Home Assistant and automate everything is such a joy.
I should have started with Proxmox from day one
It does it all (and so much more)
, nor is it the best Linux distro for beginners. In fact, it will probably encourage you to dive even deeper into those subjects. Things such as hardware passthrough, storage pools, backups, and clustering can still become complicated and still trip me up to this day. Running local LLMs is brilliant if you can get all the stars to align; otherwise, you're in for a world of pain. The difference is that Proxmox gives you a far better foundation from which to tackle them.
I would likely encounter the same or other problems with another platform, and the web UI included with Proxmox makes it easy to manage everything. If I want to test a new service, I can create an isolated environment, experiment with it, and delete the entire thing if it doesn't work out. Snapshots and backups also make it much easier to recover when an update, configuration change, or questionable late-night idea goes wrong. Honestly, snapshots are so good that I stick with them for migration too.
I no longer have to decide whether a server will be dedicated to storage, smart-home management, media streaming, or general self-hosting before installing an OS. I know what I'm going to be using as the underpinning glue to hold everything together. Proxmox lets the hardware take on several roles at once, while still keeping each workload reasonably organized and isolated.
But starting with Ubuntu Server wasn't a mistake. If I had used Proxmox earlier, I would have gained the same Linux experience without limiting the entire server to a single operating system. After rebuilding everything from scratch, Proxmox has become the part of my home lab I think about the least, and it can prove challenging to view that as the end goal. Whether you're starting with an old desktop or planning a multi-node cluster, it's the OS setup I wish I had chosen from the very beginning.
results.summary:
Proxmox Virtual Environment serves as a versatile, cost-effective hypervisor for home labs, allowing users to consolidate storage, self-hosted applications, and virtualization tasks into a single, manageable management interface.

### Key Points
- Proxmox enables users to run multiple operating systems and services, such as TrueNAS and Home Assistant, on a single hardware foundation.
- The platform features a web-based user interface that simplifies remote management compared to traditional command-line-only Linux distributions.
- Users can utilize snapshots and isolated environments to safely experiment with new software without risking the stability of the entire server.
- A three-node cluster setup can operate a full home lab, including data storage and smart home automation, for approximately $450 in annual electricity costs.
- The hypervisor supports advanced features like hardware passthrough, clustering, and containerization, providing a scalable path for both beginners and experienced users.

### Why it Matters
Adopting a hypervisor like Proxmox allows home users to replace multiple subscription-based cloud services and dedicated hardware with a consolidated, energy-efficient local data center. This approach significantly reduces long-term utility and software costs while providing greater control over personal data and home automation infrastructure.

results.title: How Long Do Owners Say ASUS Laptops Last?
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Sead Fadilpasic)
results.content:
How Long Do Owners Say ASUS Laptops Last?
Tech prices keep rising and rising. Since there seems to be no end in sight (the demand for chips will only get bigger, courtesy of AI), this is perhaps the best time to buy a new laptop. Yet, your quest to get ahead of the curve ain't easy, as there are simply too many manufacturers to choose from. The saving grace is that you can keep analysis paralysis to a minimum by choosing any of the laptop brands with a strong reputation for reliability, such as ASUS. The question is how many years is this? How long do owners say ASUS laptops last on average?
According to owners across multiple online threads, the average is around five years. Put differently, sticking with an ASUS-branded laptop is an overall safe choice across the variety of its series. This includes top-of-the-line ASUS Zenbook models and the more budget-friendly Vivobook. Gaming laptops like the ROG or TUF are equally reliable, with the ROG models surviving for over five years (although their batteries are useless at that point, according to users), and TUF getting a similar mileage.
However, not all is rosy. Some owners say their ASUS laptops died long before the five-year mark and report having a terrible experience with the brand. For instance, a user complained about a ROG laptop dying after just two years from overheating. Other gamers noted their laptop (TUF series) lasted eight years. Of course, unhappy users are more likely to put a brand on blast if they had a bad experience, which can skew the data toward the negative.
What do users complain about with ASUS laptops?
Any way you slice it, running across a bad piece of tech is always possible regardless of the brand, as one user points out. It's also easy to ignore praise from, say, an owner of an ASUS Zenbook that survived for eight years and form an opinion based on the comments of people who complain about the so-called three-year "death timer." Is there an inherent flaw?
Well, one user discouraged another from purchasing a Vivobook because it sports an OLED screen, claiming their machine bit the dust within a year. At the same time, you can find a Reddit thread where users are saying their OLED screens are still fine (without any burn-in issues) after two years. The screen complaint may not be the rule, but there are plenty of users voicing their frustration with the network cards in ASUS-branded laptops. For example, a happy ASUS stan praises the reliability of the TUF series machine but notes they had to replace a shoddy network card. A user responded by saying they experienced the same issue, and in another thread altogether, a Redditor remarked that their TUF laptop was running since 2019 with the only flaw being the Wi-Fi card.
Elsewhere, there are complaints about motherboards frying on some ROG models, with one user reporting that their high-end ASUS experienced a motherboard failure after two and a half years. Again, a handful of bad experiences don't necessarily mean that the brand is unreliable. Case in point: in a single Reddit thread, the top comment is someone who labels ASUS as decent. Scroll down a bit, and you'll find someone badmouthing ASUS and praising Lenovo, with a commenter then adding that Lenovo is a bad choice because their laptop went "crazy" after eight months.
Can you extend a laptop's life?
Even though owners maintain that ASUS laptops can last five years, there's an important factor to consider if you want a new machine to fall under this average: maintenance. Happy users seem to have a knack for taking care of their laptops. In one Reddit thread, an owner wrote that an ASUS ROG can last five years, given you periodically open it and clean the fans. Others shared extra nuggets of wisdom, like a Redditor going by 'Particular-Eye-4290' who recommends keeping the laptop on a platform to control the temperature, and avoiding using it in bed as the cushioning can block vents. They even advised keeping an eye on any temperature increases. If cleaning the debris around the fans doesn't resolve the problem, they say changing the thermal paste is a good idea.

results.title: Generative Bionics' smart robot skin prevents collisions
results.author: Omar Kardoudi
results.content:
Humanoids and humans are increasingly sharing factory floors, but one is made of metal and the other of flesh and bones, a mismatch that rarely ends well for us in a collision. Italian startup Generative Bionics thinks it has a fix: a humanoid robot covered in sensing skin that feels people approaching and adjusts its movements before any contact occurs.
The robot, called Gene.01, is wrapped in a network of sensors running from its torso to its limbs. This smart skin tracks touch, temperature, proximity, and force simultaneously, letting the robot anticipate a person's presence and react before and during contact. It's a bit like pulling your hand away from a hot stove before you actually touch it. The heat you feel from a distance is enough to make you stop.
The same sensors let humans physically teach the robot new tasks. Rather than only showing Gene.01 a movement on video, a person can guide its arm directly, helping it learn exactly how much force to apply. Generative Bionics says this solves one of humanoid robotics' persistent headaches: teaching a machine to grip an object firmly enough that it doesn't drop it but gently enough that it doesn't crush it – a skill that's hard to learn from video alone.
Gene.01 has grown out of research from the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT), published recently in Nature Machine Intelligence, and the company says it's the first industrial platform to apply this peer-reviewed method to a fully functional, sensor-covered humanoid.
The robot was built using a concept called Physical AI, which treats a robot's body, mechanics, and movement control as one integrated system rather than building the hardware first and programming intelligence into it afterward, as is traditionally done. Generative Bionics says this lets it simultaneously tune both the robot's hardware and its movement intelligence based on measurable factors like ergonomics and walking stability, using models of both the robot and the humans it will work alongside.
Rather than a single finished product, Gene.01 is designed as a base platform for a family of specialized robots. Customization happens on three levels: tailoring the AI to a specific task, adapting the exterior design to the work environment, and swapping end effectors – the technical term for hands, grippers, or feet – depending on the job.
The company's ambitions extend beyond one robot and beyond hardware alone. Generative Bionics wants to build a sovereign European ecosystem for Physical AI, complete with trusted supply chains and its own compliance standards. To that end, it's struck a strategic alliance with German firm Synapticon to develop a European-made, EU-protected chain of actuators (the motorized joints that give robots their movement), with final assembly, calibration, and safety testing all done on European soil.
"Unlike other one-size-fits-all humanoids, Gene.01 is a scalable platform, customized at the edge of AI, design, and end-effector level to maximize each customer's needs," said Daniele Pucci, CEO of Generative Bionics. "Our goal is to amplify humans with robots that can sense, feel and learn from the physical world – and adapt to the specific industrial work each customer needs."
The company's confidence is backed by real money – Generative Bionics has raised an US$81 million seed round led by CDP Venture Capital, with participation from AMD Ventures, Duferco, Eni Next, RoboIT and Tether. The first real-world application is already underway, with the company partnering with shipbuilding giant Fincantieri to develop a welding humanoid for use in its shipyards.
Source: Generative Bionics

results.title: Texas Man Texts With Potential Fort Worth Landlord. Then He Asks Him To Download Something Suspicious
results.author: charlottecolombo
results.content:
TikTok has arguably changed the property market game. But one Texas man almost became the victim of a scam after a house looked too good to be true.
As previously reported by BroBible, there is a problem with real estate scams at the moment. But this TikTok, which has garnered 28,000 views, is arguably an even bigger red flag.
In a 10-minute-long video, TikTok user Matthew Daniels (@matthewdaniels073) began by explaining how he found a potential home to rent on TikTok. Showing viewers the image, it was presented as a four-bed, with two and a half bathrooms. It was listed as having a $1,000 deposit and $1,149 rent.
He and his wife decided to go for it, so he texted the landlord and set up a time to view the home. Daniels went on to note how he asked standard landlord questions, such as about felonies, which he answered honestly. When he asked the landlord why the price was low, they said it was because it was hard getting people to pay the higher price.
They Visit The Property
They decided to see the property. When he and his wife arrived, they were asked to sign into what looked like the Invitation Homes website with a username and password the landlord texted over. However, it kept failing. Daniels also noted that while the TikTok profile had a white man’s picture, the landlord sounded Indian on the phone.
According to Daniels, the landlord started getting irritated when verification didn’t work. He asked him to download the app and make his own account to pass verification, which he did. Through this, he got a code for the door. The door opened, and Daniels and his wife looked through the “beautiful” two-storey home.
He asked the landlord again why it was so cheap, and he said nobody was paying or interested in the higher price.
Things Got Sketchy
Things took a turn when Daniels found the same address on the app. On the app, the house was listed as being $2,200 per month. He asked the landlord about the discrepancy, and he tried to explain it away by citing moving fees, application fees, and deposit. But this was inconsistent with the breakdown of the $2,200 charges on the app. At this point, Daniels asked the landlord why he wasn’t here. He said he was out of town.
In turn, Daniels said if he wants the house, he wants to pay the cash in person. While the landlord agrees with this, he says that if he wants to be considered, he still needs to pay the application fee.
The Scam Was Exposed
Once he leaves, Daniels gets emails about a house that appears to be from Invitation Homes. He calls the number on the email to say he found a house on TikTok, but what happened next is shocking. The worker said they don’t advertise on social media, and that the man is a fraud, as there are no individual landlords.
Daniels then showed the landlord’s TikTok feed on his phone to the camera. The feed is full of similar posts about houses to rent. He remarks that he’s scamming “so many people.”
Ultimately, he encouraged viewers to be “careful” about this “new type of scam.” He remarked that he almost got “hustled.”
“If you don’t feel at peace with something, if something ain’t right. And of course, and something I know if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is,” he said.
Daniels encouraged viewers to share this. He also looked through the account again and pointed out how many posts there were of houses all over Texas. As well as this, he showed how many people were commenting on these posts.
BroBible reached out to Daniels via TikTok direct message and Invitation Homes via email.
People Were Alarmed
Commenters commiserated with him.
“Anytime something looks to good to be true usually is,” one wrote.
“Sometimes even the comments are scammers too, or bots,” a second warned. “They add those comments so it can look verified.”
“Yup, anything on TikTok concerning homes is a fraud,” a third agreed.
While a fourth said, “PLEASE be careful opening any links, whether they’re in an email or text. I used to work for a major bank. they now have it to where simply clicking a link can install malware onto your phone or computer. they can then see all information in your phone. your pictures, saved passwords and your banking info, etc. your phone could already be compromised since you clicked the link that guy sent you.”
Woman Finds Own Condo For Rent On TikTok
Back in February, one woman had their own sore experience with a TikTok realtor—she discovered a video on the app which appeared to advertise her home as being for rent.
“This is my loft that I bought with my fiancé in 2024,” she said in her own video overlaying the advertisement. “This is my exact unit. Not for rent.”
The user then reached out to this TikToker to explain that her home wasn’t for rent. She shared the conversation with viewers.
“Not understanding why you are texting me?” the “realtor” wrote.
“Because you just posted a video of my house saying it’s for rent and it very much is not,” the TikToker responded.
The realtor replied, “A house and a apartment is two different things for one. Secondly I don’t care where you live I didn’t ask. Its not your house first off.”
However, the TikToker was blocked when they tried to respond further.
“Mind you, yes, this is actually my loft,” they insisted. “I own it.”

### Key Points

- The scammer directed Daniels to a fake login page mimicking the legitimate Invitation Homes website to harvest personal credentials and install potential malware.
- Invitation Homes confirmed they do not advertise rental properties on social media and do not utilize individual landlords for their listings.
- The scammer’s TikTok account featured numerous listings for properties across Texas, indicating a widespread effort to deceive prospective renters.
- Security experts warn that clicking suspicious links sent via text or email can compromise sensitive banking information and personal data stored on mobile devices.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing danger of social media platforms being used to facilitate sophisticated real estate fraud. As scammers increasingly leverage viral content to target renters, consumers must verify listings through official company websites to avoid financial loss and identity theft.

### Key Points
- The federal government has acquired equity stakes in 28 private companies since early 2025 to exert influence over corporate operations.
- In August 2025, the administration secured a 10 percent equity stake in Intel using funding provided through the CHIPS Act.
- A June 2025 executive order granted the president veto power over U.S. Steel operations following its acquisition by Nippon Steel.
- The Cato Institute reports that federal corporate welfare spending now exceeds $181 billion annually.
- New tariff policies implemented in April 2025 have contributed to increased costs for small businesses and higher consumer prices.

### Why it Matters
This shift toward state-directed corporatism represents a significant departure from traditional free-market principles in the United States. By blurring the lines between government authority and private enterprise, these policies fundamentally alter the economic landscape and impact long-term market competition.
